# Bounded measure in groups generated by a trinomial root and cyclotomic values

<a id="statement"></a>
## A uniform bound for the minimum coefficient length

For \(n\ge2\), let \(\beta_n>1\) be the positive root of \(F_n(X)=X^n-X-1\).
Fix a finite set \(S\) of positive integers and let \(\Phi_q\) be the \(q\)-th cyclotomic polynomial.
In \(K_n=\mathbb Q(\beta_n)\), consider the multiplicative group generated by \(-1,\beta_n\), and the nonzero values \(\Phi_q(\beta_n)\) for \(q\in S\).
Write \(m(u)\) for logarithmic Mahler measure and \(\lambda(u)\) for the least sum of absolute coefficients of any nonzero integer polynomial vanishing at \(u\).
For every \(B\ge0\) there is a finite bound \(L(S,B)\) such that every algebraic unit \(u\) in these groups with \(m(u)\le B\) satisfies
\[
                                \lambda(u)\le L(S,B).                    \tag{1}
\]
The bound holds simultaneously for all \(n\) and all integer exponents of the generators.
The unit assumption is on the resulting \(u\).

More precisely, \(\Phi_2(\beta_n)=1+\beta_n=\beta_n^n\), so every group element can be written
\[
                u=\pm\beta_n^a\prod_{q\in S\setminus\{2\}}
                             \Phi_q(\beta_n)^{b_q}.                       \tag{2}
\]
For \(m(u)\le B\), the units admitting (2) with some nonzero \(b_q\) form a finite set as \(n,a,(b_q)\) vary.
For the pure powers of measure at most \(B\) with \(a\ne0\), one has both \(\lambda(u)\le3^{|a|}\) and \(|a|\le B/\log\theta\), where \(\theta>1\) satisfies \(\theta^3-\theta-1=0\).

<a id="inputs"></a>
## The conjugates of the positive root

The [dominant-root argument](Yin_C_G0345_v189.md#family) with support \(0,1,n\) gives a nonreciprocal unit \(\beta_n\) whose positive powers have full degree \(d_n=[K_n:\mathbb Q]\), and
\[
                    \log\theta\le m(\beta_n)\le\tfrac12\log3.
\]
In particular the relation \(F_n(\beta_n)=0\) has no vanishing proper subset of terms.
The [bound on the support width](Yin_C_G0345_v189.md#upper) gives \(n\le 2d_n\log3/\log\theta\).
Hence \(d_n\) tends to infinity and \(h(\beta_n)=m(\beta_n)/d_n\) tends to zero, where \(h\) denotes absolute logarithmic height.
Let \(\mu_n\) assign mass \(1/d_n\) to each conjugate of \(\beta_n\).
The sequence is strict in the one-dimensional torus since each \(\beta_n\) is nontorsion and all proper algebraic subgroups there are finite.
By [Bilu's Theorem 1.1](../audits/literature/Bil97/Yin_U001.md#strict-small-points-and-orbit-measures), \(\mu_n\) converges weakly on \(\mathbb C^\times\) to Haar probability \(\mu\) on the unit circle.

<a id="height"></a>
## A height bound uniform in the exponents

Set \(I=(S\setminus\{2\})\cup\{2\}\).
There are \(c_S>0\) and \(N_S\) such that for \(n\ge N_S\) every algebraic unit (2) satisfies
\[
            h(u)\ \ge\ c_S\left(\frac{|a|}{n}
                          +\sum_{q\in S\setminus\{2\}}|b_q|\right).        \tag{3}
\]
For \(q\in I\) put \(\ell_q(z)=\log|\Phi_q(z)|\) away from its zeros.
The identity \(\gamma^n=1+\gamma\) at each conjugate \(\gamma\) gives \(\log|\gamma|=\ell_2(\gamma)/n\).
Define \(v_2=a/n\) and \(v_q=b_q\) for the other indices.
Since \(u\) is a unit, the sum of its archimedean logarithms over the embeddings of \(K_n\) is zero, and its height is the mean of their positive parts.
Consequently
\[
                2h(u)=\int\left|\sum_{q\in I}v_q\ell_q(z)\right|
                                     \,d\mu_n(z).                         \tag{4}
\]
This computes the height even if \(u\) belongs to a proper subfield, because every embedding of that subfield occurs equally often.

Choose a continuous radial cutoff \(\rho\) supported in \(1/2\le|z|\le2\), equal to \(1\) on the circle and taking values in \([0,1]\).
Set
\[
               \chi(z)=\rho(z)\prod_{q\in I}\min(1,|\Phi_q(z)|).
\]
Each function \(g_q=\chi\ell_q\) extends continuously by zero at the cyclotomic zeros, since \(t\log t\) tends to zero as \(t\) decreases to zero.
These functions are bounded and compactly supported.
On the circle \(\chi\) is positive away from the finite union of the zero sets.
If \(\int|\sum v_qg_q|\,d\mu=0\), continuity gives \(\sum v_qg_q=0\) everywhere on the circle.
Dividing by \(\chi\) away from its zeros and approaching a primitive \(j\)-th root shows \(v_j=0\) for every \(j\in I\), since only \(\ell_j\) diverges there.
Thus the integral is positive on the compact coefficient sphere \(\sum|v_q|=1\) and has a positive minimum there.

The integrals of \(|\sum v_qg_q|\) against \(\mu_n\) converge uniformly on this sphere to their integrals against \(\mu\).
Indeed weak convergence gives the result at a finite coefficient net, and \(\max_q\|g_q\|_\infty\) bounds the Lipschitz constant in the coefficient \(\ell^1\) norm for all the probability measures involved.
For all sufficiently large \(n\) the integrals are therefore bounded below by half the positive minimum.
Using homogeneity and \(0\le\chi\le1\) in (4) proves (3).

<a id="finite"></a>
## The finite set and the pure powers

If any \(b_q\ne0\), its integrality makes the right-hand side of (3) at least \(c_S\).
The identity \(m(u)=[\mathbb Q(u):\mathbb Q]h(u)\) then gives degree at most \(B/c_S\) for \(n\ge N_S\).
For the finitely many smaller \(n\) we have the degree bound \(d_n\).
There are only finitely many algebraic units of bounded degree and logarithmic measure at most \(B\), since the elementary symmetric functions of a degree-\(d\) unit's conjugates bound each minimal-polynomial coefficient in absolute value by \(2^d e^B\).
This proves the finite-set assertion and bounds \(\lambda\) on those elements.

For \(u=\pm\beta_n^a\) with \(a\ne0\), power stability, invariance of degree under inversion or negation, and homogeneity of height give \(m(u)=|a|m(\beta_n)\).
With \(j=|a|\), the product \(\prod_{\zeta^j=1}F_n(\zeta T)\) is a nonzero polynomial in \(T^j\) with integer coefficients.
Its coefficients are rational algebraic integers by Galois invariance, and replacing \(T\) by any \(j\)-th root of unity times \(T\) leaves the product unchanged.
Its coefficient length is at most \(3^j\) by submultiplicativity.
Written as a polynomial in \(T^j\), it vanishes at \(\beta_n^j\).
Reversing its coefficients or substituting \(-X\) gives the needed relation for the inverse or the negative with the same length.
For \(a=0\) the possible signs have relations of length \(2\).
Together with the finite set this proves (1).

<a id="ratio"></a>
## The ratio of the two linear translates

In particular \(\gamma=(\beta_n-1)/(\beta_n+1)\) is a unit.
The denominator is \(\beta_n^n\), and the numerator is a unit because the minimal polynomial divides \(F_n\) in \(\mathbb Z[X]\) and \(F_n(1)=-1\).
The inverse fractional linear transformation shows that \(\gamma\) has degree \(d_n\).
As the denominator has norm of absolute value \(1\), its conjugates give the stronger explicit estimate
\[
   m(\gamma)=\sum_{\sigma:K_n\hookrightarrow\mathbb C}
          \log\max(|\sigma\beta_n-1|,|\sigma\beta_n+1|)
      \ \ge\ \tfrac12d_n\log2 .
\]
Indeed the larger of the two squared distances from any \(z\) to \(1,-1\) is at least their mean \(1+|z|^2\ge2|z|\), and \(\prod_\sigma|\sigma\beta_n|=1\).
